He has to decide whether he remembers the route or only remembers seeing it.

Easy practice often loses its value in exactly that moment. A repeated route can become smooth because the world keeps handing over the same cues. The learner feels stronger, but some of the strength belongs to the current arrangement. Change the snowfield, close the notes, start the music from the bridge, or freeze the dashboard, and the pleasant feeling has to prove itself.

Matt Brown could not reread the manual at eleven thousand feet. When the right engine in his twin-engine Cessna started losing oil pressure on a night flight out of Harlingen, Texas, the tolerances and procedures had to be available without the page. In jet training, even a flat Cessna 401 fuel-system schematic became real when a pilot described ice clogging fuel filters at 33,000 feet and the need for Prist antifreeze. The diagram mattered because it connected to a decision that might have to be retrieved under pressure.

The useful question is plain: what would still be available if the support disappeared?

Q1. A dental assistant has reread the sterilization protocol three times and says it feels obvious. The supervisor wants proof she can use it tomorrow when the binder is not open. Which check fits the learning standard best?
   a) Ask her to explain the sequence with the binder closed, then check and repair the missing step.
   b) Have her reread the protocol once more and highlight every warning line.
   c) Ask whether she feels confident enough to perform the sequence alone.

Q2. A firefighter recruit runs the same hose drill ten times in a row and looks faster each round. On Saturday the route changes and his speed collapses. What was the weak signal in the original practice?
   a) The drill used physical movement instead of written review.
   b) The repeated route created fluency that depended on the same cues staying in place.
   c) The recruit should have practiced longer before any variation was added.

Q3. A student says she learned a chemistry unit because the diagrams look familiar and she remembers where each definition sits on the page. Which next move would give the most honest evidence?
   a) Copy the diagrams again in cleaner ink.
   b) Reread the definitions until their page locations are even clearer.
   c) Close the source and explain one reaction pathway on a blank sheet, then compare it with the diagram.

Q4. A sales trainer notices that new reps perform well when objections arrive in the same order as the script, but stumble when customers ask out of sequence. What practice change best follows from durable-learning standards?
   a) Mix objection types and require reps to identify the objection before using the script.
   b) Let reps repeat the script in order until they can say it faster.
   c) Replace role-play with a written quiz about the script headings.

Q5. A violinist can play a piece smoothly from the first bar but fails whenever her teacher starts her at the bridge. What does this show about the earlier practice?
   a) The bridge is too difficult and should be removed until the rest is perfect.
   b) The smooth opening may have been carrying memory forward rather than proving each passage was available.
   c) The teacher should avoid surprise starts because they damage confidence.

Q6. A trainee closes the manual and cannot recall half the equipment shutdown steps. She feels the recall attempt was a waste because it was uncomfortable. What is the best interpretation?
   a) The discomfort proves the method is bad and she should return to rereading only.
   b) Any painful study method is automatically superior to an easy one.
   c) The miss is useful if it identifies exact steps to repair and retrieve again later.

Q7. A software team studies an incident runbook every Friday with the page open. During a real outage, search is down and nobody can name the containment order. Which redesign best fits the lesson?
   a) Keep the same reading meeting but require everyone to attend in person.
   b) Add a short closed-source recall round, check the order, and revisit missed steps after a delay.
   c) Rewrite the runbook in friendlier language so it feels easier to read.

Q8. A teacher worries that making students retrieve yesterday's material before review will feel less smooth than showing the answer first. Why might the rougher opening be stronger?
   a) It makes students anxious enough to study harder next time.
   b) It removes support and reveals what memory can recover before the page starts helping.
   c) It guarantees every student will remember the answer permanently.

Q9. A certification coach must choose between two final review plans. Plan A is a calm reread of all notes. Plan B is a mixed set of closed-note problems, delayed checks, and targeted repair. Which is stronger and why?
   a) Plan A, because covering all notes once more ensures the whole syllabus is visible.
   b) Both are equal if students spend the same number of minutes studying.
   c) Plan B, because it tests recall, transfer, and weak spots after support is removed.
